# Performance

Clifft is built for fast, exact simulation of near-Clifford circuits. Its
compiler resolves Clifford coordinates, symbolic dependencies, and
output-specific sampling plans before sampling, then executes only the remaining
branch values and dense active-state operations—sharing coefficient evolution
across shots that follow the same quantum trajectory.

The measurements below cover three complementary questions: how Clifft compares
with other CPU simulators across single-core and eight-core budgets, how its
throughput has changed across releases, and how it behaves when a circuit
becomes fully dense.

## CPU simulator throughput

The [`clifft-bench`](https://github.com/unitaryfoundation/clifft-bench)
suite measures attempted shots per second for 18 complete circuits on one and
eight pinned physical CPU cores across two output endpoints:

- **Packed samples (postselection off):** return bit-packed detector and
  observable records for every attempted shot across all 18 workloads.
- **Survivor counts (postselection on):** discard shots that fail postselected
  detectors and return aggregate survivor and logical-error counts across the
  10 postselected workloads.

Clifft uses its public default compiler (`clifft.compile()` with automatic
[global reconstruction](compilation.md#global-reconstruction-for-sampling) and
bounded [active-width scheduling](compilation.md#active-width-scheduling)) and
automatic sampling selection (`batch_size="auto"`, `sharing="auto"`), with no
per-circuit manual tuning.

{{ throughput_widget() }}

Use the controls above to switch between **Packed samples** and **Survivor
counts**, toggle between **1 core** and **8 cores**, or filter simulators.
**Each panel uses its own logarithmic scale**, and scales remain fixed as
simulators are toggled. The collapsible table retains all measurements,
compile times, first-call warmups, and 8-core speedups.

Across the peer-compared workloads, Clifft leads **Tsim 1.0.0** on **10/10**
survivor-count circuits (at both 1 and 8 cores) and **12/16** packed circuits
on 1 core, rising to **16/16** on 8 cores; leads **SymFT 2026.10.8** on
**7/7** survivor-count circuits (both 1 and 8 cores); leads **Stim 1.16.0** on
its single matched workload (1-core packed `Surface code d7, r7`); and leads
**xtim 4.1.2** on **4/4** eight-core survivor-count circuits (**1/4** on
1-core survivor counts and on packed samples).

- **Magic-state preparation:** On 15-to-1 distillation, compiler simplification
  collapses the active state to width `0`, reaching **179 million** (1 core) and
  **701 million** (8 cores) packed shots/s, and **733 million** / **1.21
  billion** survivor shots/s. On Reed–Muller, Clifft reaches **93.1 million**
  (1 core) and **481 million** (8 cores) packed shots/s (vs. **22.8 million**
  and **150 million** in Tsim). On fold-transversal `d=3` and `d=5`, Clifft
  leads Tsim in both modes—reaching **89.7 million** packed and **161 million**
  survivor shots/s at `d=3` on 8 cores (**5.73x** and **7.77x** Tsim's rates).
  On cultivation `d=3`, `d=5`, and end-to-end cultivation `d=5`, Clifft leads
  Tsim across every mode and core count (up to **213 million**, **90.5
  million**, and **6.76 million** survivor shots/s on 8 cores) and leads xtim
  across all four xtim-supported circuits on 8-core survivor counts, while xtim
  is faster on packed `d=3` and `d=5` cultivation and 1-core survivor
  cultivation. On Cain 15-to-1 (`d=5` and `d=9`), 1-core packed throughput is
  close to Tsim (**929 thousand** vs. **929 thousand** at `d=5`; **271
  thousand** vs. **344 thousand** at `d=9`), while 8-core scaling puts Clifft
  ahead (**4.70 million** vs. **1.51 million** at `d=5`; **1.24 million** vs.
  **756 thousand** at `d=9`).
- **Surface-code memory and coherent noise:** On coherent `d=3, r=3`, Clifft
  reaches **10.2 million** (1 core) and **75.6 million** (8 cores) packed
  shots/s (vs. **9.45 million** and **16.9 million** in Tsim) and **140
  million** survivor shots/s on 8 cores. On coherent `d=5, r=5`, Clifft leads
  by an order of magnitude or more: **16.5 thousand** / **129 thousand** packed
  shots/s (**19.4x** / **36.7x** Tsim) and **695 thousand** / **4.96 million**
  survivor shots/s (**50.9x** / **67.2x** Tsim).
- **Arithmetic and code switching:** On the fixed-input 16-bit Draper adder,
  Tsim leads on 1 core (**403 million** vs. **235 million** packed shots/s),
  while Clifft scales ahead on 8 cores (**795 million** vs. **599 million**).
  The measured `BT27` and `BT81` code-switching circuits (no peer measurements)
  reach **230 thousand** / **1.75 million** (`BT27`) and **2.09 million** /
  **12.3 million** (`BT81`) packed shots/s on 1 and 8 cores.
- **Quantum Volume:** Dense circuits drive active width to the full qubit count
  (`10` and `20`). Shared unitary-prefix execution lets Clifft lead Tsim at
  both `QV10` (**2.68 million** vs. **2.15 million** on 1 core; **15.7
  million** vs. **519 thousand** on 8 cores) and `QV20` (**11.7** vs. **4.04**
  on 1 core; **24.4** vs. **1.29** on 8 cores).

### Clifford surface code with Stim

On the Clifford `Surface code d7, r7` workload with postselection off (packed
detector and observable records on 1 core), both Clifft and Stim return native
bit-packed detector and observable arrays directly. Clifft reaches **7.70
million shots/s** compared with **858 thousand** for Stim (**8.98x**), while
Tsim reaches **8.08 million** and xtim reaches **12.9 million**. On 8 cores
(Stim is single-threaded), Clifft scales to **56.2 million** packed shots/s
(ahead of Tsim at **42.2 million**, behind xtim at **67.5 million**) and
**68.0 million** survivor shots/s (ahead of Tsim at **60.7 million**, xtim at
**51.4 million**, and SymFT at **27.8 million**).

### Measurement setup

Rates count median attempted shots per second over three timed repetitions of
at least 15 seconds each, measured after compilation and one full warmup
sampling call (both reported separately in the widget details and data table).
Any later lazy planning remains inside the timed window. Each case runs in a
fresh worker process with thread caps applied before simulator imports.

Benchmarks run on AWS `m7a.4xlarge` instances (AMD EPYC 9R14, Ubuntu 24.04)
using one or eight pinned physical CPU cores and a 32 GiB memory limit. The
comparison covers **Clifft 0.14**, **Tsim 1.0.0**, **xtim 4.1.2**, **SymFT
2026.10.8**, and **Stim 1.16.0**; see the
[Clifft v0.14 results](https://github.com/unitaryfoundation/clifft-bench/tree/8f1c023d963b2b05316cc074ade7542c8925c950/results/release-clifft/0.14.0rc3-20261124-0148),
[peer simulator results](https://github.com/unitaryfoundation/clifft-bench/tree/8f1c023d963b2b05316cc074ade7542c8925c950/results/release-v1/0.14.0rc1-20261120-2134),
[review summary](https://github.com/unitaryfoundation/clifft-bench/blob/8f1c023d963b2b05316cc074ade7542c8925c950/results/release-clifft/0.14.0rc3-20261124-0148/report/review.md),
and [benchmark contract](https://github.com/unitaryfoundation/clifft-bench/blob/8f1c023d963b2b05316cc074ade7542c8925c950/docs/benchmark-contract.md)
for exact software commits, environments, and timing boundaries.

## Changes in v0.14

![Clifft v0.14 survivor-count throughput ratios over v0.13 on one and eight cores side by side: gains on all nine paired circuits, ranging from 1.08x to 65.0x](../assets/performance/release-change-light.png#only-light)
![Clifft v0.14 survivor-count throughput ratios over v0.13 on one and eight cores side by side: gains on all nine paired circuits, ranging from 1.08x to 65.0x](../assets/performance/release-change-dark.png#only-dark)

Across all nine paired survivor-count workloads, Clifft v0.14 improves
throughput over v0.13 at both core counts, ranging from **1.08x** to **65.0x**:

- **Fold-transversal `d=3`** reaches **65.0x** v0.13 throughput on 1 core and
  **54.9x** on 8 cores.
- **Cultivation `d=5`** reaches **61.1x** (1 core) and **58.2x** (8 cores), and
  **end-to-end cultivation `d=5`** reaches **43.1x** (1 core) and **29.3x**
  (8 cores), with global reconstruction lowering peak active width from **10 to
  6** on both circuits.
- **Coherent `d=5, r=5`** reaches **49.6x** (1 core) and **45.7x** (8 cores) at
  peak active width `13`.
- **Cultivation `d=3`** (**11.1x** / **9.83x**), **coherent `d=3, r=3`**
  (**7.34x** / **6.62x**), **85q distillation** (**5.71x** / **5.33x**),
  **surface code `d=7, r=7`** (**2.47x** / **2.45x**), and **15-to-1
  distillation** (**1.74x** / **1.08x**, reaching **1.21 billion shots/s** on
  8 cores at width `0`) all improve as well.

Fold-transversal `d=5` appears in the peer comparison above (**7.94 million**
and **59.9 million** survivor shots/s on 1 and 8 cores); its v0.13 survivor
baselines were omitted from the paired campaign because of their runtime.

Three changes drive the v0.14 gains:

1. **[Global sampling reconstruction](compilation.md#global-reconstruction-for-sampling)**
   (`reconstruction="auto"` by default) builds narrower output-specific sampling
   plans, cutting peak active width on circuits such as `d=5` cultivation from
   10 to 6 and folding redundant rotations.
2. **[Shared trajectory execution](cpu-execution.md#shared-trajectory-execution)**
   (`sharing="auto"` by default) reuses quantum state evolution across shots
   following equivalent trajectories, prunes postselected shots early, packs
   shared states into contiguous slabs, and reuses idle worker pools across
   calls.
3. **Runtime SIMD dispatch and default scheduling:** packed batch kernels
   dispatch to AVX2 and AVX-512 at runtime, and `clifft.compile()` now enables
   a bounded [active-width scheduler](compilation.md#active-width-scheduling)
   by default.

## Performance over time

While the comparison above measures v0.14 against v0.13 on the expanded
benchmark suite, the historical series below tracks a consistent six-workload
QEC core from v0.1 through v0.12. Clifft's compiler-and-executor separation
allows each release to improve circuit optimization, symbolic planning,
executable preparation, or active-state kernels without moving circuit analysis
back into the per-shot execution loop.

![Median Clifft throughput from v0.1 through v0.12 relative to v0.1](../assets/performance/performance-over-time-light.png#only-light)
![Median Clifft throughput from v0.1 through v0.12 relative to v0.1](../assets/performance/performance-over-time-dark.png#only-dark)

The first major step arrived in [v0.8](../updates/symbolic-sampling.md), when
symbolic plans replaced the original localized-Pauli virtual machine. Version
[0.10](../updates/packed-sampling.md) combined compiler width reduction with
packed sampling—including an 837x gain on coherent `d=5, r=5` after reducing
peak active width from 24 to 13. Version [0.11](../updates/less-work-per-shot.md)
added operation scheduling and deferred noise sampling, and version
[0.12](../updates/smaller-active-states.md) preserved that QEC throughput while
adding state-aware compiler simplification, reaching a **13.6x median speedup
over v0.1**.

The v0.1 through v0.9 points come from a common
[history execution](https://github.com/unitaryfoundation/clifft-bench/tree/59f78d280c5fcb90f42cc75cfd73ff3f004ad4e8/results/clifft-history-v1/clifft-history-v1-20260902),
and v0.10 through v0.12 chain paired release ratios onto that baseline as
recorded in
[reporting sources](https://github.com/unitaryfoundation/clifft-bench/blob/59f78d280c5fcb90f42cc75cfd73ff3f004ad4e8/reporting/sources.json).

## Dense Quantum Volume circuits on 16 cores

Whereas the Quantum Volume rows above compare near-Clifford samplers at `QV10`
and `QV20`, this multi-core study compares Clifft against dedicated statevector
simulators (**Qiskit Aer**, **qsim**, and **Qulacs**) up to `QV28` ($2^{28}$
amplitudes) where Clifft's near-Clifford representation offers the least help.

![Execution time for dense Quantum Volume circuits in Clifft, Qiskit Aer, qsim, and Qulacs](../assets/performance/quantum-volume-light.png#only-light)
![Execution time for dense Quantum Volume circuits in Clifft, Qiskit Aer, qsim, and Qulacs](../assets/performance/quantum-volume-dark.png#only-dark)

Using 16 physical CPU cores on an AWS `c8i.8xlarge` (**Clifft 0.10**), Clifft
records the shortest median execution time at `QV20` and `QV22`. At `QV28` it
completes in 24.7 seconds, compared with 29.9 seconds for Qiskit Aer and 344.9
seconds for Qulacs; qsim leads from `QV24` onward and finishes `QV28` in 11.4
seconds. Smaller widths favor tools with lower fixed startup overhead. Even
outside its intended near-Clifford regime, Clifft remains competitive with
dedicated statevector simulators.

Following the original Clifft paper's protocol, Clifft's timer includes
compilation plus one sample, while Qiskit transpilation and Qulacs/qsim circuit
preparation occur before their timers. Each width uses three circuit seeds; see
the [experiment description](https://github.com/unitaryfoundation/clifft-bench/blob/566924f2638a04d87cffa5930a91f3b4b3a48ee7/experiments/qv/README.md)
and [complete result table](https://github.com/unitaryfoundation/clifft-bench/blob/566924f2638a04d87cffa5930a91f3b4b3a48ee7/experiments/qv/results/qv-0.10.0rc1-20260902/cases.csv).
